---
title: "Rotation and Angular Momentum"
---

**Objectives**

- **Observe and Describe** phenomena associated with rotation and angular momentum.

The mathematical and physical description of rotating objects is fascinating and full of
surprises. In this lab, you will carry out a variety of experiments to investigate many of the
phenomena associated with rotation. There are **three experiments:**

1. Rolling Objects
1. Moment of Inertia
1. Gyroscope

Do all of these experiments. For each, **observe & describe** the system as accurately as you
can. The goal this week to to make detailed qualitative observations. Record your observations
in your notes. Make diagrams and sketches. Try to interpret what you observe using the concepts
of torque, angular momentum, and moment of inertia when you summarize your findings in this
week's memo.

## Key Ideas

This section briefly describes the fundamental quantities in rotating systems.

**Angular Momentum:** For a single particle, angular momentum is defined as
$$\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}$$
Angular momentum is a *vector* that depends on both the position and momentum of a particle. It
points in a direction perpendicular to both. To find the direction of the angular momentum
vector, curl the fingers of your *right hand* in the direction of rotation. Your thumb will point
in the direction of the angular momentum vector.

**Conservation of Angular Momentum:** Like energy and momentum, angular momentum is a quantity
that is conserved in all interactions. This concept is the key to understanding many of the
phenomena in today's lab.

**Moment of Inertia:** For a collection of particles like a wheel or pulley, we describe the
collective rotational motion with two quantities: the **moment of inertia** $I$ and the **angular
velocity** $\vec{\omega}$.
$$\vec{L} = I \vec{\omega}$$
The angular velocity describes both the direction and speed of rotation. The moment of inertia
depends on how the mass of an object is distributed about the rotation axis. The moment of
inertia of a single particle rotating around an axis distance $R$ away is $$I = mR^2.$$ The total
moment of inertia of an object is the sum of contributions from all of the particles that
comprise it.

**Torque:** Just as a *force* is required to change the *momentum* of an object, a *torque* is
required to change the *angular momentum* of an object. Torque is defined as a *moment of force:*
$$\vec{\tau} = \dfrac{\Delta \vec{L}}{\Delta t}
\qquad \qquad
\qquad \qquad
\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$$

You are not expected to be an expert on these topics, but try to use these concepts in describing
the phenomena you observe in today's lab.

## Rolling Objects

For this experiment, we will use a ramp and a collection of spherical or cylindrical objects. The
objects have different masses and mass distributions. Some are hollow and some are solid.

Make a set of observations to determine what factors affect how quickly an object rolls down a
ramp. Compare pairs of objects side by side and try to answer the following questions. Answer
them with **experimental observations** — not speculation or theorizing.

- How does the **radius** of an object affect its acceleration down the ramp?
- How does the **mass** of an object affect its acceleration down the ramp?
- How does the **shape** of an object affect its acceleration down the ramp?
- Which factors have the strongest influence on the acceleration?

## Rotating Platform

This set of experiments will allow you to experience torque and angular momentum directly. As
you work through these activities, **observe and describe** the effects and your sensations. No
measurements are required. Try instead to explain the phenomena in terms of torque, angular
momentum, angular velocity, and moment of inertia.

- Step on the platform without causing it to rotate. While you are standing on the platform, try
  to make yourself rotate. What happens? Why?

### Moment of Inertia

Stand on the rotating platform. Spin yourself or have your partner spin you — slowly at first.
Raise and lower your arms as you spin.

- What happens to your rotational speed? What quantity are you changing, and why does this
  affect your motion?

Now grab a pair of $\SI{1}{kg}$ weights — one in each hand. Raise and lower your arms as you are
spinning.

- What happens to your rotational speed this time? Why does a little extra mass make such a
  difference?

### Bicycle Wheel

- Hold the bicycle wheel. Give it a spin. Try to rotate the spinning wheel. What happens? Why?

Next, (carefully) stand on the rotating platform. Have your partner hand you the bicycle wheel.
Start with both the bicycle wheel and yourself at rest.

- What happens as you or your partner make the bicycle wheel spin?
- What happens as you change the orientation the spinning bicycle wheel?

Draw some simple sketches that illustrate the effects you observed. Try to illustrate the angular
momentum vectors of yourself and the bicycle wheel.

## Gyroscope

Each table has a pair of gyroscopes. Play with a gyroscope for a while. The fascinating behavior
of a gyroscope is a consequence of conservation of angular momentum.

### Observation

- Observe and describe the behavior of a spinning gyroscope. Describe how it moves or something
  interesting you can do with it.
- Draw a simple sketch that depicts the angular momentum vector of a spinning gyroscope.

### Precession

If you set a gyroscope spinning, tilt it at an angle, and set it on a table or a post, the
gyroscope undergoes **precession.** It will maintain a constant angle as it rotates, without
falling over. Make some detailed qualitative observations of this phenomenon.

- How does the rate of precession depend on the tilt angle? The rate at which the gyroscope is
  spinning?
- If two gyroscopes are spinning in opposite directions, will they also precess in the opposite
  directions?

## Above and Beyond

The following activities are not required. If you have the time and the inclination, you may
carry out these investigations for extra credit. You are also free to use any of the materials
available in the lab to carry out your own investigations. You need to **keep a record of your
work** (setup, procedure, data, analysis) to get credit for your efforts.

**Gyroscope Analysis:** Draw a free body diagram of a precessing gyroscope. Indicate all forces
acting on it. Draw another diagram that shows the angular momentum vector and the net torque on
the gyroscope. Use your diagrams to explain why the spinning gyroscope precesses instead of
falling over.

**Quantitative Study:** Make quantitative measurements of any of the phenomena you investigate in
this lab. Record and analyze numerical data. For example, measure the acceleration of an object
rolling down a ramp, or the rate of precession of a gyroscope, then analyze your findings.

**Moment of Inertia:** Design and carry out an experiment to measure the moment of inertia of a
pulley in the lab.

**Mathematical Modeling:** Make a quantitative mathematical model of your experience on the
rotating platform. Estimate your moment of inertia and the changes when you raise and lower your
arms. Are the predictions of this model consistent with your experience? If not, try to improve
the model.
